$comment: MANAGED IDENTITIES AND DATA-PLANE ROLE ASSIGNMENTS. One identity per deployable.
Rights come from a role assignment on the resource, not from a credential the application holds.
That is the whole point: they are centrally revocable, visible without reading application
configuration, and there is nothing to exfiltrate. build/policy/azure-identity.json is the rule;
this file is where it is discharged.
LEAST PRIVILEGE IS EXPRESSED HERE, NOT ASSUMED. The two deployables deliberately do NOT get the
same set. The monolith is read-only (ADR-0001) and its identity is what makes that structural
rather than a convention: it holds no Service Bus, SignalR, AI Search or model access at all, so
a write path added to it by mistake fails at the platform rather than succeeding quietly.
ROLES ARE NAMED, NOT NUMBERED. Built-in role names are what `az role assignment create --role`
accepts and what a reviewer can check; the GUIDs are resolved at deploy time. A GUID transcribed
into a repository is a value nobody proofreads.
TWO RESOURCES ARE NOT RBAC AND ARE CALLED OUT BELOW rather than left to be discovered:
PostgreSQL authorizes at the database level, and Redis uses an access policy. Writing either as
a role assignment produces a deployment that succeeds and an application that cannot connect.

identities.name: id-synthia-monolith
$comment: THE READ-ONLY DEPLOYABLE, and its role set is the shortest in this file on purpose.
It serves customer and staff read surfaces over versioned views and writes nothing. It
therefore holds no Service Bus role (it publishes and consumes nothing), no SignalR role (it
notifies nobody), no AI Search role (it retrieves nothing) and no model access (it reasons
about nothing). Each absence is a control, not an oversight: ADR-0001 says this deployable
is read-only, and an identity that could send a message would make that a promise rather
than a property.

roleAssignments.why: Resolves the secret references in its container app manifest at revision start.
Entra-authenticated telemetry ingestion, so no instrumentation key is held.
Pulls its own digest-pinned image. Read-only, and on the registry alone.

identities.name: id-synthia-integrations
$comment: THE ONLY IDENTITY THAT CAN READ A CONNECTOR CREDENTIAL, and the only one with an egress
path to a customer system (ADR-0007, spec 21.6). Everything below follows from that.
WHAT IT HOLDS THAT NOTHING ELSE DOES: `secret:synthia-connector-*`. Per organisation, per
system, resolved at the point of use and never written back. This scope was WITHDRAWN from
id-synthia-ragcore in the same change rather than duplicated here - duplicating it would
have left the orchestrator able to read them and made the split cosmetic.
WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT HOLD, each absence being a control:
- NO SignalR role. Notification is RagCore's leaf; this service notifies nobody.
- NO AI Search role. It retrieves nothing.
- NO model or Foundry access, and no AI Gateway route. It does no reasoning
(FR-INTEG-007), and a model client here would be a second, ungoverned egress outside
the gateway's metering, budgets and content safety.
- NO Service Bus role on `synthia-triggers`. That queue carries approval and consent
triggers, which move work past a human decision. This service makes no such decision
and must not be able to forge one.
- NO Service Bus SENDER role on the command queue, and no RECEIVER on the results queue.
It consumes commands and publishes results, never the reverse: a service that could
dispatch work to itself would be executing without a job row RagCore wrote.
ITS DATABASE RIGHTS ARE NOT HERE. PostgreSQL authorization is a GRANT, applied by migration
0021 to the `synthia_integrations` principal: write on the `integration` schema it owns,
SELECT on exactly two published views, and no base-table access at all. Recorded there
rather than here because the database enforces it, and a role assignment in this file
would read as though Azure did.

roleAssignments.why: Resolves its own platform secret references - the database DSN, the Application Insights connection string - at revision start.
Resolves per-organisation, per-system CONNECTOR credentials at the point of use. THE ONLY IDENTITY WITH THIS SCOPE; withdrawn from RagCore rather than shared with it.

Entra-authenticated telemetry ingestion, so no instrumentation key is held. Reports under its OWN service name, so it is a distinct telemetry source while the platform's single correlation identifier still spans the journey (FR-DEMO-028).
Consumes commands. Receive only, and scoped to the queue: a namespace-scoped role would reach the approval triggers. Declared with the queue in build/infra/messaging/queues.json.
Publishes outcomes through its own transactional outbox. Send only, on the results queue alone.
Pulls its own digest-pinned image. Read-only, and on the registry alone.

identities.name: id-synthia-ragcore
$comment: THE EXECUTION LEG. Orchestrates, persists, publishes and consumes, so its set is larger -
and every entry below is one it genuinely exercises.
It holds BOTH Service Bus Sender and Receiver because it is both ends of the outbox seam: the
dispatcher publishes and the workers consume. Data Owner would cover both in one line and is
deliberately not used - it also grants management of queues and subscriptions, which nothing
here does.
IT HAS NO DIRECT MODEL ACCESS. Every model call goes through the AI Gateway, which holds its
own identity onward to Foundry (build/policy/azure-identity.json, resource `foundry`). A
Foundry role here would be a second path to a provider that bypasses the gateway's metering,
budgets and content safety - the exact thing the gateway exists to prevent.

roleAssignments.why: Resolves ITS OWN platform secret references - the database DSN, the SignalR endpoint, the Application Insights connection string - at revision start.
$comment: NARROWED FROM VAULT-WIDE TO A PREFIX ON 2026-09-18 (ADR-0007, spec FR-INTEG-016).
THIS NARROWING IS THE CONTROL, NOT A TIDY-UP. While this was `scope: vault`, RagCore
could read every secret in the vault - including every organisation's CONNECTOR
credentials for ServiceNow, Graph, OneLogin and Duo. RagCore is the component that
processes untrusted model output, retrieved content and chat text by design, so that
made an orchestrator compromise a credential breach for every customer system. It is
the specific risk 18.2 and 35.2 record as accepted, and this is the half of it that
ADR-0007 discharges.
THE ROLE IS WITHDRAWN, NOT DUPLICATED. Connector secrets are named
`synthia-connector-*` and are outside this prefix, so no assignment here reaches them.
id-synthia-integrations below holds that scope and is the only identity that does.
SC-DEMO-020 measures this by ATTEMPTING the resolution from RagCore and observing Key
Vault refuse - not by reading this file. A scope asserted in configuration and never
exercised is a scope that can be silently wrong.

roleAssignments.why: The outbox dispatcher publishes triggers. Scoped to the queue, not the namespace.
The workers consume them. Same queue; Data Owner is deliberately not used.
Dispatches authorized work to the Integrations Service. Send only: it must not consume its own commands.
Consumes outcomes and resumes the graph. Receive ONLY, and the absence of Sender here is a control: RagCore must not be able to fabricate a successful outcome for work that never ran.
Publishes completion notifications. A notification carries no authority (FR-IDENT-005), so this is the narrow app-server role and not Service Owner.
Retrieval only. Index authoring belongs to ingestion and is not granted here.

identities.name: id-synthia-apim
$comment: THE GATEWAY'S OWN IDENTITY, and the reason this file blocks work that is already merged.
APIM reads the gateway client certificate from Key Vault as this identity. Without the
assignment below there is no certificate on the backend connection, Container Apps ingress
rejects the handshake, and every application request fails - the edge trust boundary in
build/policy/edge-trust.json does not function at all.
It is an identity rather than a stored credential for the usual reason, which matters more
here than anywhere else in this file: a secret used to fetch the certificate that proves
gateway provenance would be a credential guarding the thing that guards everything else.

roleAssignments.why: Reads the gateway client certificate. A Key Vault certificate's private material is retrieved as a secret, so this is the role that applies - Certificates Officer would also permit issuing and deleting, which APIM never does.

$comment: NOT AN AZURE RBAC ROLE ASSIGNMENT, and the most common way this file would be got wrong.
Entra authentication to PostgreSQL Flexible Server works by presenting an access token in
the password position; authorization is then decided by GRANTs on a database role created
with `pgaadauth_create_principal`. Writing it here as a role assignment produces a deployment
that succeeds and an application that cannot connect - the failure appears at the first query
of the first request, in a place that looks nothing like a permissions problem.
The separated principals (the monolith's read-only principal, RagCore's owner, the migration
principal that alone holds DDL) are defined with the schema, not here.
Also not an RBAC role. Azure Cache for Redis and Azure Managed Redis authorize Entra
principals through a data access policy on the cache, assigned to the principal's object id.
Redis is transient-only in this platform and no sample flow reads it, so the assignment is
listed for completeness and is not on the critical path.

$unassigned: DELIBERATELY ABSENT, so that a reader can tell a decision from an omission:
Front Door - needs no identity. Its Private Link connection to APIM is approved on the
control plane at provisioning time; no data-plane call is ever made as itself.
Foundry    - reached only through the AI Gateway, which holds the identity onward. Neither
deployable has direct model access, by design.
Monolith   - holds no Service Bus, SignalR, AI Search or model role. See its entry above.
